lesson.title: Verb-Second Bootcamp
lesson.subtitle: Front adverbs and objects — the verb never leaves position 2

hook.title: The Glued Verb
hook.content: German main clauses have one load-bearing wall: the conjugated verb sits in position 2. You may front anything — Morgen lerne ich Deutsch. Das Buch lese ich. Heute wandern wir. — but the verb does not budge. Front the adverb and the subject slides right; front the object and it slides again. The wall never moves. English speakers feel this as 'weird word order'; feel it instead as what it is — the same V2 habit Old English verse used ('Hwæt! We Gar-Dena...'), still standing in German.

footnotes.title: V2 Is the Germanic Default
footnotes.content: All the old Germanic languages ran verb-second in main clauses. English lost it; German, Dutch, and the Scandinavian languages kept it. Yoda's 'Much to learn, you still have' accidentally speaks better Old English than modern English does.

pattern.title: Front Anything, Move Nothing Else
pattern.content: Neutral: Ich lerne morgen Deutsch. Fronted time: Morgen lerne ich Deutsch — verb glued at 2, subject slides to 3. Fronted object: Das Buch lese ich heute — same glue. Fronted place: Im Haus lerne ich — same glue. The subject must still appear somewhere: if it is not in position 1, it lands immediately after the verb. One warning pair: Ich will... (modal in 2, infinitive at the end) versus Willst du...? (flipped question) — both keep the verb in the wall.
pattern.linguist_note: Adverb order inside the sentence follows the famous TeKaMoLo guideline — Time, Cause, Manner, Place — but at your level one adverb at a time is plenty: Morgen lerne ich. Heute trinken wir.

exercises.prompt: Front the time: which is correct German?
exercises.explanation: Position 1 = Morgen, so the verb holds position 2 and the subject slides to third.

exercises.prompt: Match each fronted sentence with its English meaning:
exercises.target_answer: Heute trinken wir Tee, Morgen komme ich, Das Buch lese ich, Jetzt wandern wir
exercises.meaning: today we drink tea, tomorrow I am coming, the book I am reading, now we hike
exercises.explanation: Anything can take position 1 — the verb answers from position 2 every time.

exercises.prompt: Reorder into neutral order: 'Morgen komme ich' with the subject first:
exercises.explanation: Neutral order: subject first, verb second, time word third. Fronting Morgen just reshuffles around the glued verb.

exercises.prompt: Select EVERY honest English rendering of this German subordinate clause:
exercises.german: Ich weiß, dass er heute kommt
renderings: I know that he is coming today
I know that he comes today
traps: I know that today comes he
He knows that I am coming today
exercises.target_answer: I know that he is coming today
exercises.meaning: I know that he is coming today
exercises.explanation: Even though 'dass' sends 'kommt' to the end of the German clause, natural English keeps the verb right after 'he' (jetzt weiß ich es). [Ref: will]

exercises.prompt: Assemble: 'Tomorrow we want to learn German'
exercises.meaning: Tomorrow we want to learn German
exercises.explanation: Morgen (1), wollen (2), wir (3), contents inside, lernen closes — V2 and the bracket in one sentence.

summary.outcome: Front adverbs and objects while keeping the conjugated verb in position 2.

use_example.english: Tomorrow we want to learn German.

summary.takeaway: Front anything you like — the verb stays glued to position 2 and the subject slides in right behind it.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Next: weil & dass — the subclause doors where the verb finally leaves position 2 and waits in the basement.

twist.prompt: Without looking back — rebuild the core sentence from Verb-Second Bootcamp (Tomorrow we want to learn German):
twist.explanation: Re-assembling "Morgen wollen wir Deutsch lernen" from scratch locks in the structural pattern of Verb-Second Bootcamp without relying on short-term echo.

morgen.etymology_derivation: Cognate with English morrow (hence to-morrow) and morn — both descend from the Germanic root for "morning". [wiktionary]

wollen.etymology_derivation: Retains original Germanic sense of desire/intent: "free will", "will to live", "against my will", and "willingly" (cf. Latin voluntary).

müssen.context_translation: I must / have to go now.
müssen.etymology_derivation: Cognate with English "must" (root shifted to sibilant -ss-).

lernen.context_translation: I am learning German with Brücke.
lernen.etymology_derivation: Shared root *liznōną (to follow a track/learn) + infinitive -en.

trinken.context_translation: I drink a glass of water.

buch.context_translation: I am reading a good book.

haus.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *hūsą — an exact twin of English house, down to the diphthong. [wiktionary]

großeltern.etymology_derivation: groß (great) + Eltern (the elders); Eltern descends from alt, cognate with English old. [wiktionary]

schmerz.context_translation: I have pain in my back.
schmerz.etymology_derivation: Proto-West Germanic *smertan — cognate with English smart in its old 'sting' sense. [wiktionary]

entschuldigung.context_translation: Excuse me, where is the station?
entschuldigung.etymology_derivation: entschuldigen + -ung — the 'un-guilting' noun; the page names no English cognates. [wiktionary]

sicher.etymology_derivation: Borrowed very early, already in Old High German, from Latin securus (free from care); that is the same Latin word that later reached English as secure and sure. [wiktionary]

wärme.context_phrase: Ich genieße die Wärme der Sonne.
wärme.context_translation: I enjoy the warmth of the sun.
wärme.etymology_derivation: Warm plus the noun suffix -e; warm is the identical twin of English warm (Proto-Germanic *warmaz), so die Wärme is simply warmness. [wiktionary]

krankenhaus.context_translation: My uncle works at the hospital.
krankenhaus.etymology_derivation: Kranken (sick person) plus Haus (house — exact twin of English house, Proto-Germanic *hūsą); the sick house. English hospital is a Latin word, unrelated. [wiktionary]

konto.etymology_derivation: Borrowed from Italian conto, a calculation — the Latin counting-word behind English account. [wiktionary]

steuer.etymology_derivation: From Middle High German stiure (support); the page traces the sense from helm to supporting post to support money to tax and documents cognate English steer — what you pay keeps the ship of state on course. [wiktionary][dwds]

th_to_d.name: The Dental Shift (TH → D)
th_to_d.historical_linguistics: Every single original Germanic "th" sound systematically shifted to "d" in High German, while English kept the ancient "th".
th_to_d.philological_note: Around 500–700 AD in the High German Consonant Shift, dental fricatives hardened into voiced dental stops.

d_to_t.name: The Stop Shift (D → T)
d_to_t.historical_linguistics: Where English kept Germanic "d", High German hardened it into "t".
d_to_t.philological_note: Voiced stops became voiceless. Explains pairs like day ↔ Tag, door ↔ Tür, and drink ↔ trinken.
d_to_t.literature_source: Complementary to the TH → D shift: as TH took over D, original D shifted to T in High German.

p_to_pf_f.name: The Labial Shift (P → PF / F)
p_to_pf_f.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /p/ shifted to the affricate "pf" at the beginning of words, and to "f" or "ff" after vowels.
p_to_pf_f.philological_note: Explains apple ↔ Apfel, pepper ↔ Pfeffer, hope ↔ hoffen, and sleep ↔ schlafen.

t_to_s_ss_z.name: The Sibilant Shift (T → S / SS / Z)
t_to_s_ss_z.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /t/ shifted to sibilant "s/ss/ß" after vowels, and to "z" (/ts/) at the beginning of words.
t_to_s_ss_z.philological_note: Reveals water ↔ Wasser, eat ↔ essen, better ↔ besser, two ↔ zwei, and to ↔ zu.
t_to_s_ss_z.literature_source: Walter Skeat - Primary dental affrication and spirantization

k_to_ch.name: The Velar Shift (K → CH)
k_to_ch.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /k/ softened to the fricative "ch" in medial and final positions.
k_to_ch.philological_note: The Ach-Laut [x] occurs after a, o, u; the Ich-Laut [ç] occurs after e, i, ä, ö, ü.

v_to_b.name: The Bilabial Shift (V / F → B)
v_to_b.historical_linguistics: Intervocalic /v/ and /f/ in English regularly correspond to voiced /b/ in German.
v_to_b.philological_note: Explains give ↔ geben, live ↔ leben, love ↔ lieben, over ↔ über, and seven ↔ sieben.
v_to_b.literature_source: Proto-Germanic bilabial spirant closing to stop in High German

y_gh_to_g_ch.name: The Palatal & Guttural Link (Y → G & GH → CH)
y_gh_to_g_ch.historical_linguistics: English vocalized palatal "g" into "y" (say, day, yesterday) and silenced "gh" (night, laugh, light). German preserved them as "g" or "ch".
y_gh_to_g_ch.philological_note: Explains why English spelling has silent 'gh' letters — they were original German-like gutturals!

latin_ieren.name: The Latin / Romance Layer (-ate / -ize → -ieren)
latin_ieren.phonetic_rule: English verbs ending in -ate, -ize, -ify, -ish ➔ German verbs ending in -ieren
latin_ieren.historical_linguistics: English verbs derived from Latin or French directly map to German verbs ending in -ieren.
latin_ieren.philological_note: Past participles of -ieren verbs never take the "ge-" prefix (studieren → studiert).
latin_ieren.literature_source: Middle High German productive loan suffix from Old French -ier

strong_verbs_ablaut.name: The 7 Strong Verb Classes (Ablaut)
strong_verbs_ablaut.phonetic_rule: English irregular strong verbs with internal vowel changes ➔ German strong verbs following the exact same Ablautreihe
strong_verbs_ablaut.historical_linguistics: Shared 7 Proto-Germanic verb classes where tenses are formed by shifting root vowels.
